actions.text:

Onions late Feb–Apr, shallots Apr. Overwintering onions Aug.

Plant sets

Spring sets Mar–Apr. Overwintering onions Sep–Oct. Suitable shallots autumn or winter.

methods.text:
From seed 

Sow thinly in drills ⅝ in. deep. For an early start, raise single plants in modules under cover. Harden off and plant at their original level.

From sets 

Press each small bulb into a hole, root end down and tip just showing. Firm and water in. Guard against birds until rooted. Each shallot bulb needs room to divide.

text:
Onions and Shallots.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Grow onions and shallots for fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring sets offer a simple start; seed gives more choice of colour, size and season. Shallots usually form clusters; overwintered onions crop earlier. All need clean, fertile ground and thorough drying for storage. Timings and bolting risk vary.

Quick facts
Sow

Onions late Feb–Apr, shallots Apr. Overwintering onions Aug.

Harvest

Jun – Sep

Germination

21 days

Seed depth

5/8 in.

Yield (10 ft row)

8 lb

Row spacing

Between rows: Onions and shallots 12 in.; salad onions 8 in.

Plant spacing

Salad onions 1 in., seed-grown bulbs 4 in.. Onion sets 4–6 in., shallot sets 6–8 in..

Ready in

From planting: sets ~20 weeks, shallots ~18; from sowing: spring ~22, August ~46 weeks

Plant sets

Spring sets Mar–Apr. Overwintering onions Sep–Oct. Suitable shallots autumn or winter.

Recommended varieties
BULB ONIONS
Red Baron

Red bulbs for salads and cooking; available as seed or sets.

BULB ONIONS
Sturon

A dependable brown storage onion, usually grown from sets.

BULB ONIONS
Ailsa Craig

Large, mild bulbs from seed; useful in the kitchen rather than for long winter storage.

SALAD ONIONS
White Lisbon

A familiar salad onion with slender white stems; sow small batches for steady young pickings.

SHALLOTS
Jermor

A flavoursome, copper-skinned shallot with elongated bulbs, usually grown from sets.

SHALLOTS
Zebrune

A banana shallot from seed; elongated bulbs are easy to slice.

Key risks
White rot (mouldy nose)

White rot affects onions, shallots, garlic and leeks.

Allium leaf miner

Adult flies make distinctive rows of small white feeding punctures on allium leaves.

Bolting

Prolonged cold can trigger early flowering, especially in large sets or weather-checked young plants.

Leek moth

Leek-moth caterpillars can mine onion and shallot leaves and damage bulbs.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
68
ONION FAMILY

Start with clean, firm ground.

Weed gently; keep soil drained and evenly moist.

Dry storage bulbs thoroughly.

Long storage needs sound, well-ripened bulbs.

Soil & preparation
Choose open sun and fertile, firm, well-drained soil. Add well-rotted compost before planting; avoid fresh manure and excess nitrogen.
Rotate crops yearly. Rake a fine seedbed for sowing; test acid soil before liming.
Sowing & planting
Sow shallowly
Space young plants
Plant tip showing
Allow room to grow
From seed 

Sow thinly in drills ⅝ in. deep. For an early start, raise single plants in modules under cover. Harden off and plant at their original level.

From sets 

Press each small bulb into a hole, root end down and tip just showing. Firm and water in. Guard against birds until rooted. Each shallot bulb needs room to divide.

Looking after the crop
Thin seed-grown bulb onions first to 2 in., then to 4 in..
Weed shallow roots carefully; water in dry spells and mulch thinly with compost. Replant lifted sets; guard against birds.
Remove flower stems; use bolted bulbs early. Reduce watering as bulbs mature and let foliage yellow naturally. Excess nitrogen produces thick necks that store poorly.
Harvesting & storage
Pull salad onions young. Lift mature onions when leaves yellow and fall; lift and separate shallot clusters when ready.
Dry on airy trays, covered in wet weather, until necks and outer skins dry: often two weeks. Store sound bulbs cool, airy and frost-free. Discard rot; use sound damaged or thick-necked bulbs first.
Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
White rot (mouldy nose) — Yellow leaves; white mould at roots/base.	Remove diseased plants; keep alliums off infected soil.
Allium leaf miner — White puncture rows; larvae or pupae inside.	Mesh during fly activity; remove infested material.
Bolting — Flower stems before bulbs mature.	Use suitable or heat-treated sets; use bolted bulbs early.
Leek moth — Leaf mines; caterpillars inside.	Remove infested leaves; mesh rotated beds.
Downy mildew — Grey leaf mould; stunted growth.	Remove diseased growth; space well, drain and rotate.
Neck rot — Soft stored necks with grey mould.	Dry well; store sound bulbs; remove rots.
Onion fly — Yellow, drooping leaves; maggots at base.	Remove infested plants; rotate and mesh.
Rust — Orange pustules; possible yellowing.	Remove badly affected leaves; improve airflow.
Birds pulling sets — New sets uprooted.	Replant and firm; use secure, taut netting.
Bull neck (thick neck) — Thick, fleshy necks dry poorly.	Avoid excess nitrogen; use sound bulbs early.
Final tips

Unpack delayed sets and spread them in a cool, light place until planting.

Spring sets need suitable soil conditions; prolonged cold increases bolting risk.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
